table.text: The experiment was approved by the University of Chicago SSD IRB (IRB number: IRB20-1324).
All participants gave informed consent, and the study was approved by the University of Chicago Institutional Review Board (IRB20-1324).
Participants: We recruited 159 participants using the Prolific research platform.
Participants were paid $8 an hour for their participation as well as a flat $3 bonus for completing the task.
Participants completed learning blocks for each dimension sequentially (order randomized).
Multi-Dimensional Decision Task: After learning, participants completed a multi-dimensional decision task in which they were asked to choose between two multi-attribute options presented as columns.
Participants completed 120 trials, with a self-paced break (up to one minute) at the midpoint.
No feedback was provided on any trial, though participants were informed that their choices accrued points toward their bonus.

Before the main task, participants completed six practice trials with the mouse-contingent display in which they searched an occluded display for a single target stimulus ("Which side has the purple?"), familiarizing them with the aperture and the response buttons.
Participants were given 3000ms to judge which item was higher or lower according to a prompt.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

prereg_check.title: Preregistration Check

table.title: Inferring Categorical vs Relational Value Construction from Attribute-Sampling Behavior
table.research_questions:
H1: Sampling Pattern Reflect Computational Demands
Hypothesis: The two valuation policies impose distinct attentional demands. The relational policy (constructing value) is fundamentally comparative, requiring the decision-maker to toggle between options to detect local differences (akin to flipping back and forth between two similar kitchens). In contrast, the categorical policy (retrieving value) treats options as independent entities, requiring only that features be identified and their values retrieved from memory.
Prediction: On divergent trials, the relative allocation of sampling to within-dimension comparisons (vs. between-dimension transitions) will predict choice. Greater within-dimension sampling will be associated with higher probability of choosing the relational winner; greater between-dimension sampling will be associated with higher probability of choosing the categorical winner.
H2: Discriminability Shifts Sampling Strategy
Hypothesis: The efficiency of the categorical policy depends on the ability to map a visual feature to a specific value category. When perceptual discriminability is low (e.g., the features are highly similar but on opposite ends of a boundary between categories), the uncertainty of retrieval increases. To resolve this uncertainty, the decision-maker must abandon the efficient categorical strategy and engage the relational policy to resolve the difference via direct visual comparison.
Prediction: As within-dimension discriminability decreases (i.e., the two stimuli on a dimension become more perceptually similar), participants increase within-dimension sampling on that specific dimension.
H3: Individual Differences in Category Knowledge Predict Policy Reliance
Hypothesis (Main Effect): The stability of the categorical policy depends on the strength of the underlying memory representations. Individuals with robust category knowledge (stronger priors) can retrieve values more reliably and with less cognitive effort than those with weaker knowledge, leading to a general bias toward the memory-guided categorical policy.
Prediction: Participants with higher learning accuracy (category knowledge) will select the categorical winner significantly more often on divergent trials compared to participants with lower accuracy.
H3b: Knowledge Moderates the Impact of Uncertainty
Hypothesis: Strong category knowledge buffers against perceptual uncertainty. Just as an expert realtor can instantly categorize a kitchen that looks ambiguous to a novice, participants with high category knowledge should be able to maintain a categorical policy even when discriminability is reduced. In contrast, participants with weak knowledge will be forced to switch to the relational policy (comparison) more rapidly as discriminability drops.
Prediction: We predict a Knowledge × Discriminability interaction on sampling behavior. The tendency to increase relational sampling (within-dimension transitions) in response to low discriminability will be attenuated for participants with high category knowledge.

table.study_design_overview:
Learning Task: Participants learn value-category mappings for three perceptually uniform dimensions:
1.	Shape: Radial frequency patterns drawn from a validated circular shape space (Li, Liang, Lee, & Barense, 2020, J Exp Psychol Gen)
2.	Color: Hues drawn from CIELAB perceptually uniform color space
3.	Angle: Orientation of an indicator line within a circle, ranging from 0–230°
Each dimension is divided into five value categories (e.g., for a given dimension: Category 1 = 0 points, Category 2 = 25 points, Category 3 = 50 points, Category 4 = 75, Category 5 100 points). The mapping direction (ascending vs. descending along the perceptual continuum) is counterbalanced across participants.
On each learning trial, participants see two stimuli from different value categories on the same dimension and select the higher- or lower-value option (prompt alternates every 10 trials). Feedback shows correctness and reveals both values. Participants complete learning blocks for each dimension sequentially (order randomized).
Free-Sorting Task: After learning each dimension, participants perform a two-stage free-sort with 16 items spanning that dimension: first sorting by perceptual similarity, then re-sorting by value.
Novel Choice Task: Participants complete 120 trials. On each trial, two multi-dimensional options are presented as columns, each containing one stimulus from each dimension (row positions randomized but matched across columns). Participants select the option with higher aggregate value. No feedback is provided.
Our main trials of interest are those where the categorical policy and relational policy point to separate options. We label these trials divergent trials. These arise when one dimension exhibits a large value difference that outweighs two smaller opposing differences on the remaining dimensions. That single dimension is called the critical dimension. For example, if Option A scores [80, 20, 20] and Option B scores [20, 40, 40] across three dimensions, then: - Categorical winner = Option A (summed EV: 120 vs. 100) - Relational winner = Option B (wins on 2 of 3 dimensions)
As there are 3 dimensions, we will generate an equivalent number of divergent trials where the critical dimension is shape, color, and line orientation (20 trials each). Overall, there will be 60 divergent trials. There will also be an equivalent number of non-divergent trials (where both policies point the participant towards the same option), which will serve as control trials. 
Mouse-Contingent Display: Each trial begins with a 500ms full preview, after which stimuli become occluded (grey, low-resolution). Participants reveal stimuli by hovering the mouse cursor (100px aperture radius) over each location. This creates a serial processing bottleneck, allowing us to record information sampling trajectories.
table.randomization:
•	Dimension-to-feature mapping: randomized across participants
•	Value mapping direction: counterbalanced across participants
•	Dimension learning order: randomized across participants
•	Trial-level stimulus positions: randomized within constraints to achieve target divergent trial rate
table.data_collection_procedures:
Data collection: Data collection will be performed using the Prolific research platform with a jsPsych experiment posted on cognition.run. 
Pre-selection criteria: Participants will be 18–36 years old, fluent English speakers, residing in the USA, and report no problems with color vision. To ensure high quality, we will also select participants who have completed 20 or more decision-making tasks on Prolific with an average acceptance rate of 100%
Exclusion criteria (applied sequentially):
1. Incomplete Data: Participants who do not complete all blocks of the experiment.
2. Learning Failure: Participants who achieve less than 60% accuracy in the final block of the learning phase for any of the three dimensions.
3. Non-Compliance: Participants who fail to uncover any information (0 mouse-overs on stimuli) on more than 5% of novel choice trials.
table.sample_size: We plan to collect N = 80 participants after applying exclusion criteria.
table.sample_size_rationale:
We use a sensitivity power analysis (using the SIMR package) approach given uncertainty in true effect sizes from pilot data. Power analysis accounting for within-subject clustering from the pilot sample (subject standard deviation = 0.523) indicates we can detect >95% power to detect our conservative target effect (β=0.139, OR=1.15) at α=.05 if the intercept is between 0 and 2.1. These come from beta estimates run on all trials as divergent trial count was low in the pilot. Given this, a more conservative estimate would allow for N = 80 participants and approximately 60 divergent trials per participant (50% of overall trials in the novel-choice task). This represents an effect-size that is plausible given our pilot data, where we observed qualitative differences in sampling patterns across trial types despite limited divergent trial counts.
Pilot data (N = 27, ~18% divergent trials) showed directional effects consistent with H1 and H2, though confidence intervals were wide due to sparse divergent trials. The current design increases divergent trial frequency to improve precision.
table.stopping_rule: We plan to collect data as soon as this pre-registration is posted. Participant data will be run through an automated pipeline that only applies exclusion criteria. Participants will be collected on prolific until we have reached our designated sample size.
table.manipulated_variables:
- Dimension-to-feature mapping: randomized across participants
- Value mapping direction: counterbalanced across participants
- Dimension learning order: randomized across participants
- Trial-level stimulus positions: randomized within constraints to achieve target divergent trial rate
- Composition and temporal placement of divergent trials
table.measured_variables:
- choices and response times in learning task
- mouse movements and final positions in the free-sorting task
- choices, response times, and mouse movements/positions in the novel choice task
table.indices:
All sampling metrics are derived from mouse trajectory data recorded via the gaze-aperture display. 
- Sampling events occur whenever a participant uncovers part of the stimulus. As the aperture is rather wide any time the center of the aperture enters a 100px radius centered on the object is deemed a sample. 

- Within-Dimension Transitions: Count of consecutive sampling events where the participant moves from one stimulus to the other stimulus within the same dimension (i.e., comparing the two options on a single feature).
- Between-Dimension Transitions: Count of consecutive sampling events where the participant moves from a stimulus in one dimension to a stimulus in a different dimension (i.e., traversing down or across the option columns).

- Total Transitions: Sum of within-dimension and between-dimension transitions on a given trial.

- Within-Dimension Proportion: Ratio of within-dimension transitions to total transitions. Higher values indicate more relational-style sampling; lower values indicate more categorical-style sampling.

Note: Because total transitions = within-dimension + between-dimension transitions, these measures are linearly dependent. Analyses condition on total transitions or use the proportion directly.

Operationalizing category knowledge
This is a participant-level measure of how well the participant learned the underlying category-to-value mapping during the learning phase. 
Primary operationalization: mean accuracy on the final block of the learning task, averaged across all three dimensions.

Operationalizing perceptual discriminability
The perceptual distance between the two stimuli on a given dimension. For each dimension, discriminability is computed as the absolute angular difference along the respective perceptual continuum. Lower discriminability means the two stimuli are more perceptually similar and harder to distinguish.
table.statistical_tests:
Model 1: Sampling Predicts Choice (H1)
Mixed-effects logistic regression on divergent trials:
"choice relational"∼"within dimension count"+"between dimension count"+"discriminability critical"+(1+"within dimension count" |"subject" )
- choice_relational: 1 if participant chose relational winner, 0 if categorical winner
- within dimension count: count of within-dimension transitions on that trial 
- between dimension count: count of between-dimension transitions on that trial
- discriminability critical: discriminability on the critical dimension (covariate) 
- Random intercepts and slopes for within dimension count by subject

Model 2: Discriminability Shifts Sampling (H2)
Mixed-effects negative binomial regression on divergent trials:
"within dimension count critical"∼"between dimension count"+"discriminability critical"+(1+"discriminability critical" |"subject" )
- within dimension count critical: count of within-dimension transitions on the critical dimension 
- discriminability critical: discriminability on the critical dimension 
- between dimension count: count of between-dimension transitions across all dimensions 
- Random intercepts and slopes for discriminability_critical by subject

Mixed-effects logistic regression on divergent trials:
"choice categorical"∼"category knowledge"+"discriminability critical"+(1|"subject" )
- choice categorical: 1 if participant chose categorical winner, 0 otherwise 
- discriminability critical: discriminability on the critical dimension
- category knowledge: participant-level learning accuracy (between-subjects predictor) 
- Random intercepts by subject

Model 3b: Knowledge Moderates Discriminability Effect (H3b)
Mixed-effects negative binomial regression on divergent trials:
"within dimension count critical"∼"total transitions"+"discriminability critical × category knowledge"+(1+"discriminability critical" |"subject" )
table.transformations: As response time is not normally distributed it will be log-transformed before being used in exploratory analyses.
table.inference_criteria:
H1 Inference: H1 is supported if the coefficient for within dimension count is positive and statistically significant (p < .05)

H2 Inference: H2 is supported if the coefficient for discriminability critical is negative and statistically significant (p < .05).

H3a Inference: H3a is supported if the coefficient for category knowledge is positive and statistically significant (p < .05).

H3b Inference: H3b is supported if the interaction coefficient is positive (i.e., the negative discriminability→sampling relationship is attenuated for high-knowledge participants).
table.data_exclusion_criteria:
Data Preprocessing
1.	Compute value sums for each option on each trial; classify trials as divergent or non-divergent
2.	For divergent trials, identify the categorical winner, relational winner, and critical dimension
3.	Extract sampling metrics from mouse trajectory data: within-dimension transitions, between-dimension transitions, total transitions
4.	Compute discriminability for each dimension on each trial
5.	Compute participant-level category knowledge scores

Exclusion criteria (applied sequentially):
1. Incomplete Data: Participants who do not complete all blocks of the experiment.
2. Learning Failure: Participants who achieve less than 60% accuracy in the final block of the learning phase for any of the three dimensions.
3. Non-Compliance: Participants who fail to uncover any information (0 mouse-overs on stimuli) on more than 5% of novel choice trials.
table.missing_data_handling: As long as participants meet our inclusion criteria we will use all available data from them and ignore missing data.
table.exploratory_analyses:
1.	Divergent vs. non-divergent comparison: Test whether sampling patterns (within-dimension proportion) differ systematically between divergent and non-divergent trials.
2.	Free-sort alignment: Examine whether Adjusted Rand Index from the value-based free-sort predicts choice policy and/or sampling, as an alternative operationalization of category knowledge.
3.	Endpoint effects: Verify that discriminability effects are not driven by stimuli near the perceptual dimension endpoints (0° or 230°).
4.	Response time: Examine whether RT on divergent trials relates to sampling pattern and/or choice, potentially indicating strategy conflict.

data_check.summary_text:
-  We classified 538 files: 43 data, 486 code, 7 documentation, 2 materials.
-  We found 8 tabular data files and extracted 33 columns from 6 of them.
-  We grouped the files into 2 study groups (ex1, ex2), plus 3 collection-level files (README/ro-crate metadata).
-  2 tabular data files could not be read because they were not downloaded. This can happen for private repositories or failed downloads; you can also pass `local_path` to point at a local copy.
-  4 trial-level data files (E-Prime / Inquisit / jsPsych / Behaverse) were recognised. These are per-participant records of a behavioural task, so they are not listed as separate datasets. Nothing is deleted. We ran automated data-quality checks on 33 columns and found no issues.

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 33 columns across 6 data files.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 6 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: Participants: We recruited 159 participants using the Prolific research platform.
Participants were paid $8 an hour for their participation as well as a flat $3 bonus for completing the task.
Participants completed learning blocks for each dimension sequentially (order randomized).
Multi-Dimensional Decision Task: After learning, participants completed a multi-dimensional decision task in which they were asked to choose between two multi-attribute options presented as columns.
Participants completed 120 trials, with a self-paced break (up to one minute) at the midpoint.
No feedback was provided on any trial, though participants were informed that their choices accrued points toward their bonus.

Before the main task, participants completed six practice trials with the mouse-contingent display in which they searched an occluded display for a single target stimulus ("Which side has the purple?"), familiarizing them with the aperture and the response buttons.
Participants were given 3000ms to judge which item was higher or lower according to a prompt.
Furthermore, participants differed widely in these weights, such that participants were not all weighting the same dimension highly and the other two lower (M = +1.98, 95% HDI [+1.76, +2.18]).
If participants were using a pure directional strategy, it should not matter whether the left side wins by +25 or by +100 (Figure 4 C purple line).
If instead participants were using each value difference, one would expect an equivalent change in choice for each of the Δvalue increments (Figure 4 C orange line).

We found that participants had a wide variance in how they sampled the multi-dimensional decision task stimulus display while comparing the two options (mean -0.20, SD 0.30, range -0.80 to +0.74; 21% above 0; Figure 5 A for examples).

In literature on cue combination, participants are shown to weight dimensions according to reliability, such that dimensions that are more reliable are given higher weight in the composite stimulus (Ernst and Banks 2002; Bankieris, Bejjanki, and Aslin 2017).
All participants gave informed consent, and the study was approved by the University of Chicago Institutional Review Board (IRB20-1324).

info.title: Learning and Using Value Maps in Multi-Dimensional Choice

author.affiliation:
Institute for Mind and Biology
								The University of Chicago

Institute for Mind and Biology
								The University of Chicago

text.text: When making choices between multi-dimensional options, people draw upon knowledge of the options' various properties to make a decision.
While much work has probed how individuals make decisions in these modes, less is known of how learned value maps can be flexibly composed to support novel decisions.
Here we taught participants three separate perceptual-to-value mappings, each dividing a continuous perceptual dimension into five value categories.
We then had them choose between composite options never encountered during learning while a mouse-contingent display forced serial information sampling.
How the learned map was read during choice varied widely across people, from fully metric reads (e.g. how much better) to purely ordinal ones (e.g. which is ahead).
We find that ordinal comparison is not simply a degraded version of the same metric.
Instead, participants mix between ordinal and metric reads.
How well each dimension was learned set its weight, while how strongly learning accuracy depended on the separation between categories lowered both the weights and the metric share of the read.
Both the readout and weights left separable signatures in information search.
Learned value maps are thus composed and then read out to guide choice.
We often choose between options composed of several dimensions, relying on our knowledge of each dimension to make a decision about a new composite.
Consider two cocktails on a list, each described by its sweetness, sourness, and strength.
What a given level of sweetness or strength is worth to you is knowledge that you acquired one drink at a time.
As a result of uneven learning, you may only have a loose sense of strength but a better sense for sweetness, leading to different weighting of those dimensions when you choose a drink from the menu.
Upon encountering a new drink you can work out how much you think you will enjoy it by combining your knowledge of the different dimensions.
Previous work has uncovered a set of common heuristics individuals tend to follow to make choices in these types of situations (see Gigerenzer and Gaissmaier 2011; Busemeyer et al. 2019 for review).
text.formatted: Previous work has uncovered a set of common heuristics individuals tend to follow to make choices in these types of situations (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Gigerenzer and Gaissmaier 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Busemeyer et al. 2019</ref> for review).

text.text: These heuristics act as a general rules to combine dimensional values together to drive choice, or to flexibly halt deliberation when a threshold is reached.
Often, the specific values are either supplied by scalar values, measured by participant ratings, or estimated from preferences.

Recent work has further shown that these heuristics can be recovered from resource rational modeling where people are given differing knowledge about environmental features (Binz et al. 2022; Krueger et al. 2024).
text.formatted: Recent work has further shown that these heuristics can be recovered from resource rational modeling where people are given differing knowledge about environmental features <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Binz et al. 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Krueger et al. 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, the decision strategy emerges as a function of the environmental or instructional differences, but it still unclear how individuals may differ in how they learn about and represent the same environment.
The representation of a multi-dimensional decision space may rely on the cognitive mapping system (Gärdenfors 2004; Bellmund et al. 2018; Constantinescu, O'Reilly, and Behrens 2016).
text.formatted: The representation of a multi-dimensional decision space may rely on the cognitive mapping system <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Gärdenfors 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Bellmund et al. 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Constantinescu, O'Reilly, and Behrens 2016)</ref>.

text.text: In a decision space value would be graded and interpolable.
Further, maps would support valuation of combinations that were never explicitly experienced (Orloff et al. 2026; Park, Miller, and Boorman 2021; Theves et al. 2021).
text.formatted: Further, maps would support valuation of combinations that were never explicitly experienced <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Orloff et al. 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Park, Miller, and Boorman 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Theves et al. 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Maps also can be warped and uneven, moving beyond the simple conception of imprecision in the representation as adding noise to valuation (G. Son, Walther, and Mack 2024; Boccara et al. 2019).
text.formatted: Maps also can be warped and uneven, moving beyond the simple conception of imprecision in the representation as adding noise to valuation (G. <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Son, Walther, and Mack 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Boccara et al. 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Though the contents of cognitive maps have been well studied, how these maps are read at the moment of choice are less clear (Bottini et al., n.d.).
text.formatted: Though the contents of cognitive maps have been well studied, how these maps are read at the moment of choice are less clear <ref type="bibr">(Bottini et al., n.d.)</ref>.

text.text: In a multidimensional decision, each option can be thought of as a point in the space that a participant has not previously visited.
The value of an option can then be constructed by navigating along the dimensions to reach that point.
As people gain experience with the dimensions used in their decisions, they will necessarily have varying levels of imprecision in their internal representations.
This imprecision might simply add noise to the construction of an overall value estimate, or it might change how comparisons are made between options.
The same map can be read for the actual size of the differences along dimensions or merely used for a coarse read of direction.

For instance, if drink A is far better on sweetness and slightly worse on both sourness and strength than drink B, you might choose to go off of the overall number of attributes that drink B wins on (2/3).
If you instead take the drinks on balance, you might realize that A is a better drink overall.

Two people who like the same things and know them equally well can differ in these strategies; one asks how much better the winner is, the other only which drink wins in more of the flavor dimensions.
Here, we investigate how representations learned to varying precision guide value construction in multi-attribute decisions.
Participants first learned three separate perceptual-to-value mappings, each dividing a continuous perceptual dimension into five value categories.
They then chose between composite options assembled from all three while we recorded how they sampled the choice display.

We also examined mouse-tracking data to provide further insight into how information search coupled with learned representations following from a line of process-tracing work in decision-making (Gluth, Deakin, and Rieskamp 2026; Payne 1976; Yang and Krajbich 2023).
text.formatted: We also examined mouse-tracking data to provide further insight into how information search coupled with learned representations following from a line of process-tracing work in decision-making <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Gluth, Deakin, and Rieskamp 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Payne 1976;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Yang and Krajbich 2023)</ref>.

text.text: We find that how well participants learned each dimension predicts how they weight it when encountering new composites.
How strongly their learning accuracy depended on the separation between categories predicted how they read their map at choice, more by direction than by distance, and also lowered their weights.
Aside from choice, we find that the weighting and reading of the map leave separate traces in search processes.
Overall, this work disentangles what constituent components go into value construction in novel choice.
Differences in value construction may stem from variations in value maps and how they are combined and read from.
Participants: We recruited 159 participants using the Prolific research platform.

Of these, 30 were excluded for insufficient engagement with the mouse-contingent display: on more than 5% of choice trials, the cursor never entered any dimension's reveal aperture, indicating the participant was not using the display to sample information.

A further 20 were excluded for anomalously fast learning-phase responding: more than 20% of a participant's learning-trial response times fell below the 10th percentile of the pooled learning-trial RT distribution (computed after the mousequality exclusions above; threshold = 627ms), suggesting responses made without engaging with the stimuli.
The final N was thus 109 participants (age M = 29.5, SD = 4.9, range 18-37; 56 male, 49 female, 4 gender-nonbinary).
Participants were paid $8 an hour for their participation as well as a flat $3 bonus for completing the task.
Overall, the experimental session took 40-60 minutes.
The experiment was approved by the University of Chicago SSD IRB (IRB number: IRB20-1324).
Dimension Learning Task: Participants learned value-category mappings for three perceptually continuous dimensions.
The first of these was a shape space with morphs drawn from a validated circular shape space (Li et al. 2020).
text.formatted: The first of these was a shape space with morphs drawn from a validated circular shape space <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Li et al. 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Participants also learned value-category mappings for hues sampled from a circle in CIELAB space centered at (𝐿 * = 50, 𝑎 * = 20, 𝑏 * = 20) with a radius (chroma) of 60, with hue angle varying 1-231° to generate the category space.
The final dimension was a line angle, where participants saw the orientation of an indicator line within a circle.
The line's orientation swept a 230° arc centered on vertical, from 8 o'clock through 12 o'clock to 4 o'clock.

Each dimension was thus parameterized by an angle restricted to 1-231° of its underlying circular space, and this range was divided into five value categories spanning 30° of arc each (31 integer angles per category), separated by 20° gaps, so that category centers are 50° apart (Figure 1 B).
text.formatted: Each dimension was thus parameterized by an angle restricted to 1-231° of its underlying circular space, and this range was divided into five value categories spanning 30° of arc each (31 integer angles per category), separated by 20° gaps, so that category centers are 50° apart (Figure <ref type="figure">1 B</ref>).

text.text: Each category was assigned a point value (e.g., for a given dimension: Category1 = 0 points, Category2 = 25 points, Category3 = 50 points, Category4 = 75, Category5 = 100 points).
The mapping direction (ascending vs. descending along the perceptual continuum) was counterbalanced across participants.
On each learning trial, participants saw two stimuli from different value categories on the same dimension and were prompted to select the higher-or lower-value option.
The prompt alternated every 10 trials so as not to associate one end of the scale with more selections.
On every trial, a feedback screen indicated both correctness as well as the values of each option.
Participants completed learning blocks for each dimension sequentially (order randomized).
Each block was 40 trials in length such that participants performed 4 choices for each pairwise comparison between the categories.
Multi-Dimensional Decision Task: After learning, participants completed a multi-dimensional decision task in which they were asked to choose between two multi-attribute options presented as columns.
Participants completed 120 trials, with a self-paced break (up to one minute) at the midpoint.
On each of these trials, they were shown a 250 ms preview of two multi-attribute options, each containing one stimulus from each dimension (row positions randomized but matched across columns).
The stimuli were then occluded (gray-scaled, lowered resolution).
They could then reveal individual dimensions by hovering the mouse cursor over each location (100 pixel aperture radius).
This created a serial processing bottleneck that allowed us to record information sampling trajectories.

After sampling, participants then selected the option they believed carried the higher aggregate value by clicking a button on the bottom of the screen corresponding to either the left or right option.
Responding was self-paced up to a 2-minute limit per trial.
No feedback was provided on any trial, though participants were informed that their choices accrued points toward their bonus.

Trials were separated by a centrally placed fixation cross that participants clicked to begin the next trial; this returned the cursor to the center of the screen, equidistant from the two options, before each preview.

Before the main task, participants completed six practice trials with the mouse-contingent display in which they searched an occluded display for a single target stimulus ("Which side has the purple?"), familiarizing them with the aperture and the response buttons.
In this task, our main trials of interest are those where the magnitude calculation and the tally calculation point to different options.
We label these trials incongruent trials.
These arise when one dimension exhibits a large value difference that outweighs two smaller opposing differences on the remaining dimensions.
That single dimension is called the critical dimension.
For example, if Option A scores [100, 25, 25] and Option B scores [25, 50, 50] across three dimensions, then: Magnitude winner = Option A (summed EV: 150 vs.

text.text: 125); Tally winner = Option B (wins on 2 of 3 dimensions; Figure 2 B).
text.formatted: 125); Tally winner = Option B (wins on 2 of 3 dimensions; Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2 B</ref>).

text.text: As there are 3 dimensions, we generated an equivalent number of incongruent trials where the critical dimension was shape, color, and line orientation (20 trials each).
Overall, there were 60 objectively incongruent trials per participant.
There was also an equivalent number of non-incongruent trials (where both calculations point the participant towards the same option).
The set of trials were constructed to guarantee sufficient incongruent trials (random composites yield too few).
Knowledge measures: For each participant and dimension, we defined dimension knowledge as the mean accuracy across the 40-trial learning block acc 𝑠𝑑 .
Overall value knowledge 𝐾 𝑠 is the mean of the three values, z-scored across participants.

To measure how much distance between categories guided learning, we fit a hierarchical logistic regression of learning-trial accuracy on the category distance of the pair, with a slope per participant and dimension (logits per category step); a participant's ΔValue slope is the mean of their three slopes.

To test whether dimension knowledge and dimension weight coupled within participants, we double-centered the weights, removing each participant's overall gain and each dimension's overall learnability.
Category distance tracks both perceptual and value distance in this design, so the slope cannot separate the two.
In order to examine sampling dynamics, we first constructed areas of interest that aligned with each of the 3 attributes for both the left and right option (6 total AOIs).
Transitions were defined over the sequence of dimensional AOI visits within a trial.

At each mouse sample we determined which of the six dimensional AOIs (one per attribute per side, 100-pixelradius circles centered on each stimulus location) contained the cursor, if any; samples falling outside all six AOIs were left unassigned.

Consecutive samples occupying the same AOI were collapsed into a single visit, so that dwelling within one region did not itself generate additional transitions; a visit was retained only if its cumulative dwell reached 100 ms, which excludes brief transits through an AOI that lay on the cursor's path between two other regions (e.g., passing through the middle aperture of one option while moving between its top and bottom attributes) rather than reflecting a genuine attentional stop.
A transition was then defined as any adjacent pair of visits in this filtered, collapsed sequence (e.g., left-shape → right-shape → right-color yields two transitions).

Each transition was classified along two dimensions: whether it crossed sides (between-option, left↔right, vs. within-option, same side), and, among side-crossing transitions, whether the attribute also matched.

Only a side-crossing transition that landed on the same attribute (e.g., left-shape → right-shape) was classified as attribute-wise; a side-crossing transition that also changed attribute (e.g., left-shape → right-color, a diagonal move) reflects neither an option-wise nor an attribute-wise comparison and was tallied separately.

With 3 attributes and 2 options, each AOI has 5 possible destinations (2 within-option, 1 attribute-wise, 2 diagonal), so a searcher choosing among them at random produces within-option and attribute-wise moves at a 2:1 ratio rather than 1:1, and pooling them directly is therefore not centered on chance.
We used the Payne index (Payne 1976), adapted with the chance correction of Böckenholt and Hynan (1994), as our primary measure of scanning behavior.
text.formatted: We used the Payne index <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Payne 1976)</ref>, adapted with the chance correction of <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Böckenholt and Hynan (1994)</ref>, as our primary measure of scanning behavior.

text.text: Each total count was divided by its number of possible transitions (2 for within-option, 1 for attribute-wise) before differencing, computed per trial as (within-option/2 -attribute-wise/1) / (within-option/2 + attribute-wise/1).

Positive values thus indicate predominantly option-wise (alternative-based) search, e.g. scanning the attributes within one option before moving to the other; negative values indicate predominantly attributewise search, e.g. scanning back and forth between the two options within an attribute; a value of 0 corresponds to chance-level search rather than to an equal raw count of within-and betweenoption moves.

Along with the Payne index, we calculated sampling depth as the number of (dwellfiltered) AOI visits in a trial's collapsed visit sequence (revisits to a previously viewed AOI count as new visits), averaged across trials within participant; it indexes how much information a participant gathered per trial, independent of the between/within composition of their transitions.
We also computed, per participant and attribute, that attribute's share of aperture visits, of first reveals, and of attribute-wise comparisons.
Following prior literature, we call dimension-wise transitions attribute-wise in these analyses.
To relate search to the choice model, we fit one regression with the Payne index and sampling depth as joint outcomes and magnitude reliance, concentration, and gain entered together as predictors.
Value regressors: To generate the value regressors we first converted the 5 categories for each stimulus into a level index.
We do not use the point values directly as we estimate them within the choice model.

This means that for participant 𝑠 on trial 𝑡 and dimension 𝑑 we record the taught level of each option, 𝑘 𝐿 𝑑𝑡 , 𝑘 𝑅 𝑑𝑡 ∈ {0, … , 4}, along with the within-category position of each stimulus, 𝜑 𝐿 𝑑𝑡 , 𝜑 𝑅 𝑑𝑡 ∈ [-0.5, +0.5].

This within-category position is the stimulus's location inside its own 30°-wide category band, expressed as a signed fraction of the category with 𝜑 = 0 at the midpoint, signed so that 𝜑 > 0 always means toward the higher-value end of that dimension.
text.formatted: This within-category position is the stimulus's location inside its own 30°-wide category band, expressed as a signed fraction of the category with 𝜑 = 0 at the midpoint, signed so that 𝜑 > 0 always means toward the higher-value end of that dimension.

text.text: Because the taught point value is constant within a category by construction, 𝜑 carries no taught value at all.
Thus, it only adds weight if participants interpolate between the taught levels.

Choice model: We use the above value regressors to fit a choice model with three components.
The first is a value map (𝑢 𝑠𝑑 (𝑐)) that maps taught levels to a subjective utility estimate.
The second is a mixture (𝜆 𝑠 ) of the two readings of each dimension's difference on that map (its size or only its direction).
The third is a set of dimension weights (𝑤 𝑠𝑑 ) that sum the readings into the log-odds of choosing the option on the right.
We first estimate the value map as participants will have learned the value representations of each dimension to varying degrees.
For each participant and for each dimension, we fit a free monotone value map 𝑢 𝑠𝑑 over the five taught levels:
We pin the low end of the value map to 0 and fit 3 value category variables for each participant and dimension that define the increments between the value levels (𝜓 𝑠𝑑 ).
We then use a softmax over the fitted value category variables to make the individual participant value maps well-behaved.
The taught category levels are then combined with the within-category positions to estimate the overall value of a given option and thus the difference is:

When both stimuli fall in the same category 𝑘 𝑅 𝑑𝑡 = 𝑘 𝐿 𝑑𝑡 , the value difference is objectively 0 but we estimate 𝛾 𝑑 (𝜑 𝑅 𝑑𝑡 -𝜑 𝐿 𝑑𝑡 ), where 𝛾 𝑑 is a per dimension weight on how within-category location enters overall utility.
Note that 𝛾 𝑑 is shared across participants because we capture participant level variation in the shape of the value map using the per-participant increments (𝜓 𝑠𝑑 ).
Further, setting 𝜓 = 0 makes all four increments equal and 𝛾 𝑑 = 0 removes the within-band slope, which together reproduce a value map linear in the taught points.
Thus if the values of those parameters differ meaningfully from 0 it indicates that participants learn a warped and graded value map.
Fitted, the maps were graded rather than five flat labels: value varied with position inside a taught category at M = 0.81, 95% HDI [0.65, 0.97] of a fully graded map (Supplement S6).
There are two primary ways to read a value map, either by examining the distance or collapsing this to an ordinal read over the sign.
We provide these two reads as two separate channels to the model to guide choice.
The magnitude channel uses distance between options on the fitted value map (Δ𝑢 𝑑𝑡 ), whereas the ordinal channel keeps only which option is ahead, sign(𝑘 𝑅 𝑑𝑡 -𝑘 𝐿 𝑑𝑡 ), on the raw ±1 scale.
Because the fitted value map is strictly monotone in taught level, the ordinal channel is identical whether computed on taught points or on fitted values.

The two channels are two readings of the same difference vector and are correlated across trials (0.63), though the trial set was constructed so that 50% of trials place them in conflict (e.g. incongruent trials).
We next combine the above difference in option values using the two channels.
We use a mixture parameter (𝜆 𝑠 ) that we term magnitude reliance, which sets how the participant combines the two value channels.
At 𝜆 𝑠 = 1, only the magnitude channel is used such that a large advantage on one attribute can outweigh losses on the others.
Conversely at 𝜆 𝑠 = 0, only the ordinal channel guides choice such that the deciding factor is winning on 2/3 attributes.
Intermediate values mix the two channels.

These options are then compared and used to predict the probability of choosing the right-side option.
where 𝑎 0 + 𝜎 𝑎 𝑧 𝑎 𝑠 is a participant-specific side bias.
Weights are hierarchical, 𝑤 𝑠𝑑 = 𝑤 𝜇𝑑 + 𝜎 𝑤 𝑧 𝑤 𝑠𝑑 (dimension-specific group mean, one shared between-participant spread), and 𝜆 𝑠 = logit -1 (𝑐 0 + 𝜎 𝜆 𝑧 𝜆 𝑠 ).
For further analyses, we derive two summaries of the fitted weight vector.
The first of these is gain:
This measure indexes how strongly a participant used their value map to guide choice.
The second summary we derive is concentration (Gini coefficient of absolute weights):
This measure begins at 0 when all three weights are equal to one another and has a maximum value of 2/3 when all weight sits on one dimension.
Inference: For the inferential statistics we report a series of Bayesian hierarchical regressions.

As both the choice model and the regressions are hierarchical Bayesian models, in the remainder of the text we use the term model for the choice model variants and inferential statistics use the term regression.
All variants of the choice model used 4 chains with 1500 warmup and 1500 draws (target-accept 0.90-0.95); cross-validation refits were reduced in scale (600-1500 warmup and draws).
Throughout the paper each estimate, both for the choice model parameters as well as regression results, is reported as its posterior mean (𝑀) followed by the 95% HDI in brackets.
We use weakly-informative priors on our standardized predictors.
Participant-level predictors of a latent quantity (gain, 𝜆 𝑠 ) entered that quantity's prior inside the choice model.
We estimated these predictors at the same time as the latent parameter as correlating them with posterior estimates instead would bias the result toward zero.
R ≤ 1.008 on all fits of record, divergences 0; the full fits table is in Supplement S1.

Candidate models were compared by five-fold trial-wise cross-validation, the choice model in the main text was validated by generate-and-refit identifiability, parameter recovery, and forward posterior predictive checks (Supplement S2-S5).

Magnitude reliance 𝜆 𝑠 had high split-half reliability (0.89, Spearman-Brown corrected, with each participant's trials split into halves), and the 95% HDIs of recovered parameters covered the generating values 91% of the time (Supplement S4).
Pointer-device control: At debrief participants reported whether they had used a mouse or a trackpad (64 mouse, 45 trackpad).

Because pointer hardware changes the motor cost of moving the cursor between screen locations, and the display is mouse-contingent, we refit every analysis reported below with device included as a covariate (sum-coded, trackpadmouse), entering the choice model as a shift on both the whole weight vector and magnitude reliance.

Device was not credible on either parameter (magnitude reliance M = -0.49, 95% HDI [-1.24, +0.27]; weights M = -0.47, 95% HDI [-0.99, +0.04]) and no reported result moves: the knowledge couplings shift by < 0.01 (gain-knowledge +0.47, magnitude reliance-knowledge 0.00).

text.text: Deviations from pre-registration: We pre-registered the experiment before collecting the sample reported in this manuscript.
We report the results of the 4 pre-registered frequentist tests, and every deviation from the pre-registration, in Supplement S9.
We examined how participants constructed the value of novel multi-dimensional options when the dimensions were learned to uneven degrees.
We find that participants vary in how well they learned the dimensions both within and across participants.

That variation enters downstream value construction and choice through two different routes; how the dimensions are weighted for the composite, and how individuals read their value maps for direction or distance.
Each of these has its own predecessor in the dimensional learning task.
Finally, we find that these two routes also leave different fingerprints in the search process.
First we examined learning and found that participants learned the three dimensions unevenly.
Across participants, shape was modally learned best and line modally worst, with every pairwise difference credible (Supplement S7).

The unevenness between dimensions was also present within participants, on average, a participant's best-learned dimension beat their worst by 0.23 in accuracy (best / middle / worst = 0.88 / 0.79 / 0.66; Figure 1 C).
text.formatted: The unevenness between dimensions was also present within participants, on average, a participant's best-learned dimension beat their worst by 0.23 in accuracy (best / middle / worst = 0.88 / 0.79 / 0.66; Figure <ref type="figure">1 C</ref>).

text.text: Accuracy also rose with the value distance between the two categories being compared (group slope M = +0.18, 95% HDI [+0.12, +0.23]), and participants differed widely in how steeply it rose (SD of slopes M = +0.21, 95% HDI [+0.13, +0.30]).
This ΔValue slope is a separate measure from 𝐾 𝑠 (propagated M = +0.13, 95% HDI [-0.03, +0.29]), though it is noisy for any one participant (split-half r = 0.07; Supplement S7).
Each learning trial presented two stimuli from different value categories of one dimension.
Participants were given 3000ms to judge which item was higher or lower according to a prompt.
They were then shown a green box around their selection if they made the correct choice and a red box if they made an incorrect choice.
We showed the points values above both the selected and non-selected options to speed learning.
B. The stimulus is drawn from an angle in a circular perceptual space, cut into five value categories worth 0-100 points.
For each dimension we constrained the angles to only span from 1-231° with 20° gaps between value categories to aid in learning.

As participants learned the individual value maps with varying sensitivity to varying accuracy, we next sought to examine how these varied representations are combined in the service of the construction of a single value.

In the multi-dimensional decision task, participants viewed pairs of composite items, each composed of a novel combination of color, a shape, and a line angle, and selected the option they believed was more valuable (Figure 2 A).
text.formatted: In the multi-dimensional decision task, participants viewed pairs of composite items, each composed of a novel combination of color, a shape, and a line angle, and selected the option they believed was more valuable (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref> A).

text.text: As each of the dimensions carried a distinct value participants could use one of two methods to determine which choice was better.
They could sum the values for each dimension within each option before comparing which option has the higher sum (a magnitude difference).
They might also discard the explicit magnitude and simply compare dimensions on strength across options tallying up which option wins on more dimensions.

On congruent trials both the magnitude and tally point in the same direction but we explicitly introduce incongruent configurations on 50% of trials such that magnitude and tallybased comparisons will select different winners (Figure 2 B).
text.formatted: On congruent trials both the magnitude and tally point in the same direction but we explicitly introduce incongruent configurations on 50% of trials such that magnitude and tallybased comparisons will select different winners (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2 B</ref>).

text.text: We first examined whether participants differed in accuracy in the multi-dimensional decision task as a function of their overall value knowledge from the dimension learning task.
We fit a hierarchical logistic regression to assess the effect of value difference, value knowledge, as well as their interaction.

We found that difference in value between left and right options guided choice (|ΔValue| M = +1.82, 95% HDI [+1.62, +2.01]), and further that this slope steepened with overall value knowledge (|ΔValue| × 𝐾 M = +0.52, 95% HDI [+0.34, +0.73] ; Figure 3 A).
text.formatted: We found that difference in value between left and right options guided choice (|ΔValue| M = +1.82, 95% HDI [+1.62, +2.01]), and further that this slope steepened with overall value knowledge (|ΔValue| × 𝐾 M = +0.52, 95% HDI [+0.34, +0.73] ; Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3 A</ref>).

text.text: Participants with better dimensional learning use their value maps to drive choice than those with lower dimensional learning accuracy.
We next examined how accuracy differed for congruent and incongruent trials.
On congruent trials accuracy was generally high (mean = 0.88 , SD = 0.12).
Congruent trials allow both strategies to guide individuals to the correct answer and thus can be fairly straightforward.

On incongruent trials, where the magnitude calculation pointed towards the correct answer and the dimensiontally disagreed, overall accuracy fell to near chance (0.53) and its between-participant spread increased (0.12 → 0.20).
This indicated that participants varied widely in how much they relied on the magnitude of the value differences rather than only on their direction.
Indeed, this can be seen in the spread across the average correctness on incongruent trials across participants (Figure 3  B).
text.formatted: Indeed, this can be seen in the spread across the average correctness on incongruent trials across participants (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3  B</ref>).

text.text: Participant variation in magnitude versus direction reliance can come from two sources.
Given that participants learn the value maps, they might compose them with different weights akin to reliability weighting, but based on knowledge instead of environmental reliability.
They may also differ in how they read their maps to guide value construction and choice, relying on either magnitude of the value differences or simple ordinal directions.
We examined how participants may weight the composite option by fitting one weight per dimension per participant (weight vector: 𝑊 𝑠 ; Figure 4 A).
text.formatted: We examined how participants may weight the composite option by fitting one weight per dimension per participant (weight vector: 𝑊 𝑠 ; Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">4</ref> A).

text.text: After estimating a weight per dimension for every participant, we find that dimensions did not count equally (color M = +4.02, 95% HDI [+3.60, +4.43], shape M = +3.83, 95% HDI [+3.42, +4.22], line M = +3.11, 95% HDI [+2.71, +3.52]).
Furthermore, participants differed widely in these weights, such that participants were not all weighting the same dimension highly and the other two lower (M = +1.98, 95% HDI [+1.76, +2.18]).

We further summarize each participant's weight vector by its gain |𝑊 𝑠 |, the mean absolute weight, and its concentration, which captures how uneven the weights are across dimensions (Gini coefficient).
Given a specific set of weights to construct a composite there's also a way to read that composite.
For instance participants can use some mixture of magnitude or directional information from the map to guiding their choice.
If participants were using a pure directional strategy, it should not matter whether the left side wins by +25 or by +100 (Figure 4 C purple line).
text.formatted: If participants were using a pure directional strategy, it should not matter whether the left side wins by +25 or by +100 (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">4</ref> C purple line).

text.text: If instead participants were using each value difference, one would expect an equivalent change in choice for each of the Δvalue increments (Figure 4 C orange line).
text.formatted: If instead participants were using each value difference, one would expect an equivalent change in choice for each of the Δvalue increments (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">4</ref> C orange line).

text.text: We investigated how participants used magnitude or direction information in choice by fitting a mixing parameter (𝜆).

This models participants as integrating between the sign information used in a tally and the value differences from their map (at 𝜆 = 0 they are only using sign, at 𝜆 = 1 they are only using the map; see Methods: Choice Model).
We find that participants perform a mixture of these two reads, with a dimension won by 25 points carrying 0.40 [0.37, 0.44] of the weight of one won by 100.
When we use only the participant's fitted value map on size, a 25-point win should count for 0.25 [0.24, 0.26].
A direction-only read gives a 25-point and a 50-point win the same weight, which no value map read by size can do.
This parameter spanned nearly the full range available to it across participants (mean 0.76, min 0.14-max 0.99).
It was also reliable and recoverable (Methods).

As we examined the dimensional learning task using both general accuracy as well as distance sensitivity, we sought to understand whether the weights or the magnitude reliance during readout were guided by accuracy or sensitivity.
We expected that knowledge of the specific dimensions should alter their weighting during choice.
Meanwhile, the sensitivity to distance at learning should cause participants to be more sensitive to distance in their readout.

We tested all four couplings inside the choice model, entering each learning measure as a predictor of a participant's gain (a multiplicative scale on their weights) and of 𝜆 𝑠 , first alone and then both together (Methods:
Inference).

Overall value knowledge 𝐾 𝑠 predicted gain across participants, such that participants with better dimension learning task accuracy used the values they learned more strongly in novel choices (M = +0.13, 95% HDI [+0.07, +0.20]; with the ΔValue slope in the same model M = +0.17, 95% HDI [+0.10, +0.24]; Figure 4 B).

text.text: Knowledge and weight also coupled within participants, where the better-learned dimension carried more weight (double-centered and propagated M = +0.32, 95% HDI [+0.27, +0.36], across 327 participant × dimension cells; Supplement S7, Figure S2A).

text.text: Unexpectedly, a steeper ΔValue slope predicted lower gain (M = -0.09, 95% HDI [-0.16, -0.02]) opposite in sign to 𝐾 𝑠 .
Thus, knowing how well the participant did at the dimension learning task, and at which dimensions specifically, guides how they construct value for novel composites during choice.

We found 𝜆 𝑠 was not credibly related to 𝐾 𝑠 (M = +0.14, 95% HDI [-0.29, +0.55]; with the ΔValue slope in the same model M = +0.32, 95% HDI [-0.10, +0.73]), although the estimate rose once the slope was controlled, as the two learning measures partly mask each other.
This could be a function of the demands of the dimension learning task, which only ever asked an ordinal question.
Thus, overall value knowledge may only index order learning.
When we enter the ΔValue slope (Figure 1 C) as a predictor of 𝜆 𝑠 inside the choice model, we find it is credibly negative (M = -0.44, 95% HDI [-0.84, -0.04]).

text.text: Learning thus reached value construction by two overlapping routes.
The first of which depended on how well a dimension was learned set its weight.
Meanwhile, how strongly learning depended on separation lowered both the weights and the reliance on magnitude.
The weights and magnitude reliance were separable but not independent.

Concentration was orthogonal to magnitude reliance (M = +0.01, 95% HDI [-0.09, +0.12]) whereas gain was credibly related to it (M = +0.25, 95% HDI [+0.13, +0.36]; the full strategy plane is in Supplement S10).
If the two constructs from the model (i.e., weights and magnitude reliance) are separate, they should surface in different components of how participants searched for information.

We found that participants had a wide variance in how they sampled the multi-dimensional decision task stimulus display while comparing the two options (mean -0.20, SD 0.30, range -0.80 to +0.74; 21% above 0; Figure 5 A for examples).

text.text: Participants that rely on magnitude information are therefore performing search in a way commensurate with within-option summation.

Magnitude reliance did not credibly predict sampling depth (M = +0.08, 95% HDI [-0.10, +0.26]), but the crossing between them was positive and not credible (M = +0.21, 95% HDI [-0.02, +0.45]; Figure 5 E).

text.text: Sampling depth, meanwhile, was better predicted by concentration (M = -0.31, 95% HDI [-0.54, -0.10]; Figure 5 D).

text.text: Gain and concentration are two moments of the same three-vector and are correlated (-0.57), partly mechanically, and the contrast between them does not separate them either (M = +0.10, 95% HDI [-0.28, +0.46]).
We therefore claim that depth tracks the weight vector, and that magnitude reliance is more attuned to the pattern of sampling rather than the depth.
Allocation followed the weights dimension by dimension.

A dimension's weight predicted its share of aperture visits (M = +0.01, 95% HDI [+0.01, +0.01]), its share of first reveals (M = +0.02, 95% HDI [+0.01, +0.03]), and its share of dimension-wise comparisons (M = +0.01, 95% HDI [+0.01, +0.02]).
We added per-dimension learning accuracy to the same regression.
It added nothing given weight (M = 0.00, 95% HDI [-0.03, +0.03]) and left the weight coefficient unmoved (M = +0.01, 95% HDI [+0.01, +0.01]).
Thus the impact of knowledge on search is mediated by the fitted weights.
Search therefore separates the two constructs more cleanly than learning does.
Often when we make new decisions, we base them on knowledge learned across experience and organized in a cognitive map (Bellmund et al. 2018).
text.formatted: Often when we make new decisions, we base them on knowledge learned across experience and organized in a cognitive map <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Bellmund et al. 2018)</ref>.

text.text: There has been a great deal of research on how individuals make multi-dimensional decisions, finding a variety of strategies that appear rationally matched to the environment (Binz et al. 2022; Krueger et al. 2024).
text.formatted: There has been a great deal of research on how individuals make multi-dimensional decisions, finding a variety of strategies that appear rationally matched to the environment <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Binz et al. 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Krueger et al. 2024)</ref>.

text.text: As these studies supply attribute values directly, they leave open how people read a value map they have learned themselves.
Here, we taught participants value maps for each dimension to see how value is constructed.

We find that what is often called a single "strategy" in multi-dimensional choice bundles together two components of value construction: 1) how much each dimension counts (weight) and 2) how the product of dimension-by-dimension learning (i.e., the map) is read at choice time (by direction [which option is better] or by magnitude [how much better is one option]).

Further, we find that different aspects of the learning process affect these two components, and that each of these two streams leaves separate imprints in how participants search during value construction.
Because incongruent trials force the two ways of reading the map to disagree, and the choice model estimates both components from the same choices, the two could be separated here.

By linking performance in a separate learning phase to choices among never-seen composites, we could further connect individual differences in value construction to what was actually learned, which is not possible when values are estimated from ratings.

Previous work in the adaptive toolbox literature treats weighting and reading, among others, as selection from a repertoire, indexed to environment structure (Gigerenzer and Goldstein 1996; Payne 1976; Rieskamp and Otto 2006), and discrete strategies can emerge from a resource rational process that maps onto both envi-map by size predicts 25% (Figure 4 C), and no reshaping or warping of that map can produce the difference.

text.text: Instead, participants stably differ in how they perform their comparisons over a given representation.

The literature on cognitive maps establishes that participants consult geometric representations during value-based choice (Park, Miller, and Boorman 2021; J.-Y. Son, Bhandari, and FeldmanHall 2021) but rarely asks how that geometry is explicitly traversed during the construction of value for a novel option.
text.formatted: The literature on cognitive maps establishes that participants consult geometric representations during value-based choice <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Park, Miller, and Boorman 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr">J.-Y. Son, Bhandari, and FeldmanHall 2021)</ref> but rarely asks how that geometry is explicitly traversed during the construction of value for a novel option.

text.text: Here, better-learned dimensions carried more weight.
Differential weighting can occur due to uncertainty about the stimulus.

In literature on cue combination, participants are shown to weight dimensions according to reliability, such that dimensions that are more reliable are given higher weight in the composite stimulus (Ernst and Banks 2002; Bankieris, Bejjanki, and Aslin 2017).
text.formatted: In literature on cue combination, participants are shown to weight dimensions according to reliability, such that dimensions that are more reliable are given higher weight in the composite stimulus <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Ernst and Banks 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Bankieris, Bejjanki, and Aslin 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Another alternative is that the weights can differ due to differences in how predictive they are for reward, with participants learning to allocate attention to those dimensions that are more relevant (Niv et al. 2015; Leong et al. 2017; Maher et al., n.d.).
text.formatted: Another alternative is that the weights can differ due to differences in how predictive they are for reward, with participants learning to allocate attention to those dimensions that are more relevant <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Niv et al. 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Leong et al. 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Maher et al., n.d.)</ref>.

text.text: In our study, each dimension is equally rewarded and equally reliable but differs in how participants learn and represent them.
Thus our weighting could stem from attentional differences or from differences in internal reliability of learned value maps.
The way in which participants allocate sampling gives further evidence for an attentional mechanism.
We found that the readout and weights are dissociated in how individuals sample information during the task.

Where participants allocate their aperture tracks their weights, similarly to how gaze tracks attribute weights in attentional models of multi-attribute choice (Yang and Krajbich 2023), and which would be predicted by the weighting following attention.
text.formatted: Where participants allocate their aperture tracks their weights, similarly to how gaze tracks attribute weights in attentional models of multi-attribute choice <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Yang and Krajbich 2023)</ref>, and which would be predicted by the weighting following attention.

text.text: The amount of sampling also tracks the weight vector, consistent with search directed by attribute importance (Gluth, Deakin, and Rieskamp 2026).
text.formatted: The amount of sampling also tracks the weight vector, consistent with search directed by attribute importance <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Gluth, Deakin, and Rieskamp 2026)</ref>.

text.text: The pattern with which they moved between the dimensional cues, however, tracked the readout parameter.

Current attentional decision models link attention to how much each attribute counts (Krajbich, Armel, and Rangel 2010; Yang and Krajbich 2023; Gluth, Deakin, and Rieskamp 2026), and our results suggest they should also distinguish how the evidence gathered is read.
text.formatted: Current attentional decision models link attention to how much each attribute counts <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Krajbich, Armel, and Rangel 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Yang and Krajbich 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Gluth, Deakin, and Rieskamp 2026)</ref>, and our results suggest they should also distinguish how the evidence gathered is read.

text.text: Because sampling and readout were measured together, this design cannot tell whether attribute-wise sampling shapes the readout or the readout shapes sampling, and the two may well inform each other (Braunlich and Love 2022).
text.formatted: Because sampling and readout were measured together, this design cannot tell whether attribute-wise sampling shapes the readout or the readout shapes sampling, and the two may well inform each other <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Braunlich and Love 2022)</ref>.

text.text: In our work, the features that make the readout estimable also limit our ability to understand how individuals might calibrate their readout in response to changing task demands.
More specifically, the lack of feedback during the multi-dimensional decision task means that individuals had no signal to calibrate their readout to a more optimal strategy.
Future work can provide feedback during this task to examine whether participants adjust strategies to ongoing demands.
We further designed the task to incorporate a 50% rate of incongruent trials to better estimate the readout parameter.
If composites were instead drawn randomly, the expected rate of incongruent trials would be much lower.

Finally, while our mouse contingent aperture design allows us to examine information sampling without the use of an eyetracker it could induce a cost to serial sampling that is less present in free-viewing content.
Taken together, our findings suggest that the question of what strategy do people use to construct value from a learned map is better split into two: 1. how much does each dimension of the map count?
and 2. how is the map read?
Both can be traced to what people learned but leave dissociable marks in choice and information search.
The distinction matters because people routinely choose among new combinations of attributes they only previously learned piecemeal, such as products, job offers, or partners.

Our results imply that two people can make different decisions because they learned the dimensions relevant to choice to different degrees (i.e., they formed different maps) or because they read the same map differently, despite identical learning.
The results argue for treating learned representations and the operations performed on them as separate components within computational modeling frameworks.
The results also have implications for policies that set decision environments and choice aids.
Finally, this work highlights that learned value maps are not just stored but also composed and read out at the time of choice.
Differences in the latter steps help explain why two people with the same knowledge may nonetheless choose a different cocktail.
